To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the class NP can be characterized by the existence of a polynomial-time verifier, and (b) the class NP is equivalent to the class IP, the class of all problems for which there exists an interactive proof system in which the prover can convince a polynomial-time verifier to accept a correct solution.

(1) for any verifier, the set of all proofs for a given language member x is a member of NP; and (2) for any verifier and any language member x, there is a polynomial-time algorithm that computes a proof for x.

the class of languages that can be recognized in polynomial time is equal to the class of languages whose members have a polynomial number of proofs, and that the class of problems for which the optimal solution can be found in polynomial time is the class of problems whose solutions have a polynomial number.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: for a given language in NP, how much information is needed in order to decide membership?
the following question: given an NP language L and a polynomial-time verifier for L, what can be said about the set of proofs induced by the members of L?
the following problem: Given a verifier V and a set of proofs P, determine if P is a set of proofs for some member of the language accepted by the verifier.

the class NP is precisely the class of sets of proofs for a given verifier.

the class NP is the class of all sets of proofs of a verifier that can be verified in polynomial time, and the class coNP is the class of the complements of such sets of proofs.
In the present paper, we consider the inverse of the above statement: for a fixed verifier, what are the sets of proofs that can be verified by the verifier, and what are the properties of such sets of proof?
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are interested in characterizing the class of all sets of proofs induced by members of a language in NP.
we study the following question: what is the complexity of the inverse problem of deciding whether a given set is the set of proofs for a given member of the language.
we have developed a theory of inverse NP problems, that is, problems of finding a proof of membership in an NP language.
The main takeaway from our work is that

this view of NP can be reversed: for every NP problem, we can find a verifier that accepts only members of the language, and whose induced proofs are the set of witnesses to the non-membership of the language.
the set of proofs for an NP language is a polynomially bounded inverse NP problem.
the set of proofs for a member of an NP language is itself a NP language.
